46779-pottery-and-porcelain-from-early-t:
Pottery and Porcelain, by Charles Wyllys Elliott, was published in New York in 1878. Its span runs from early times to the Philadelphia Exhibition of 1876. One hundred and sixty five pictures fill the book. The more important marks and monograms are given too. A Wedgwood Portland vase forms the front plate. Elliott says his aim was to gather the key facts in a way easily understood. He wrote for the student and the collector alike.

Much matter came from Europe, where love of old china ran high since Queen Anne's day. American collections were used where he could. He defends collectors against busy men who call a hobby a waste. Knowledge of pottery, he argues, now counts as part of a liberal education.
62235-preserving-louisiana-s-legacy-ever:
Nancy Hawkins of the Division of Archaeology wrote this booklet, Preserving Louisiana's Legacy, number five of the Anthropological Study series. The state's Department of Culture, Recreation and Tourism published it at Baton Rouge in April 1982. A photograph shows a preserved Indian mound in Pointe Coupee Parish, ringed by pasture.

An editor's note by State Archaeologist Kathleen Byrd dates Louisiana's cultural heritage to about 10,000 years before Christ, when Paleo-Indian hunters entered the region after Pleistocene big game. Unlike earlier volumes, this one describes no single group or site. It explains in general terms how an archaeologist studies the past, and what factors threaten or protect archaeological remains. It tells how government, industry, business, landowners, and ordinary citizens can each help preserve the state's archaeological heritage. The booklet was printed at thirty cents a copy for public distribution.
72995-the-treatises-of-benvenuto-cellini:
Benvenuto Cellini set down his craft rules in treatises on gold work and on large carved work. C R Ashbee wrote the long opening account of Cellini and his place as a maker. The English text addresses the metal workers of the Guild of Handicraft. Chapters move step by step through each branch of the shop.

Early chapters teach niello, fine wire work, and enamel. Next come jewels and how to set a ruby, an emerald, or a sapphire. Cellini tells how to cut and tint a diamond. Later parts cover seals, coins, and medals. Big plate, vases, and figures larger than life close the gold work. Gilding and its colors end the run of lessons.
britannica-1911-kelp:
Kelp is the ash made by burning various kinds of seaweed. It is got in great plenty on the west coasts of Ireland and Scotland and on the coast of Brittany. The weeds used include the deep sea tangle, the sugar wrack, and three kinds of Fucus, the knobbed, black, and bladder wracks.

The Laminaria weeds give drift weed kelp, got only when storms cast them up on the shore. The Fucus kinds grow within the tidal range and are cut from the rocks at low water, so they are known as cut weeds. The weeds are first dried in the sun. They are then gathered into shallow pits and burned until they form a fused mass, which is sprinkled with water while hot to break it into handy pieces. A ton of kelp comes from 20 to 22 tons of wet weed.
britannica-1911-stolp:
Stolp is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Pomerania, and a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it. The town stands on the Stolpe river, ten miles from the Baltic Sea. It lies sixty four miles west of Danzig on the railway to Stargard. Its count in 1905 came to 31,154 people.

The great church of St Mary, with a lofty tower, dates from the fourteenth century. A Renaissance castle of the sixteenth century now serves as a prison. A town gate, restored in 1872, also survives from old times. These are memorials of the days when Stolp prospered as a member of the Hanseatic League. Industry in the town covers machinery and amber goods. Tobacco, cigars, and bricks are made there too, with iron founding and linen weaving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-p:
Our Lady of Perpetual Succour, also called Our Lady of Perpetual Help, is a picture painted on wood with a gold ground. Byzantine in style, it is thought to date from the thirteenth century. It shows the Mother of God holding the Divine Child. Archangels Michael and Gabriel hold out the instruments of His Passion. Greek letters above the figures shorten the names Mother of God, Jesus Christ, and the two archangels.

A pious merchant carried it to Rome late in the fifteenth century and willed it to a church for public honour. It hung at San Matteo on the Via Merulana for nearly three hundred years, drawing crowds and many graces. French troops destroyed the church in 1812, and the picture lay hidden and neglected for over forty years. Between 1863 and 1865 it was found again in an Augustinian oratory, and devotion to it spread anew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ou:
The Sisters of Our Lady of Perpetual Help began in the parish of Saint Damien, Bellechasse, Quebec, Canada, on 28 August 1892, founded by Abbé J. O. Brousseau. The institute teaches children in country and city parochial schools and educates orphans. From the first year the sisters conducted the principal schools of the Saint Damien parish.

Virginie Fournier, a woman of experience and courage from Fall River, Massachusetts, became first superior as Mother Saint Bernard and governed six years with great success. Demand grew so fast that in 1907, lacking free sisters, they refused direction of seventeen municipal schools. The first profession came on 27 March 1897, when fifteen sisters pronounced the three vows. By 1911 the order counted 112 professed sisters conducting 21 schools in Quebec with 2,532 pupils.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WitnessesAlphab: J. W. Masland compiled an alphabetical listing of Warren Commission witnesses. The commission heard from hundreds of people in 1964, and finding one name in that mass was slow work without an index. Masland's list turns the witness roll into a research aid. It remains useful to any reader who wants to move from a name to testimony in the commission's volumes.
nasa-tm-19690020347-the-molecular-kineti:
James O. Ballance of Marshall Space Flight Center analyzes vacuum gauge behavior in this April 1969 report. The gauges are the Bayard-Alpert type and a modified Redhead magnetron type. Both flew on the Explorer 17 and Explorer 32 satellites to measure upper atmosphere density.

A Monte Carlo computer analysis traced the free molecular flow inside each gauge. Transmission probabilities were found for simplified gauge shapes. A similar approach had already given very valid results for a sounding rocket mass spectrometer gauge, Ballance notes. Effects of specular reflections from gauge walls were examined. A simple time response model of the gauges was also determined. Better gauge models mean better density data from satellite flights.
